title: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
summary: How a database caches disk pages in a buffer pool, why plain LRU and CLOCK collapse under sequential scans, and how LRU-K, 2Q, PostgreSQL's clock-sweep and InnoDB's midpoint insertion protect the hot set.
outcomes: Explain how a buffer pool serves a page request using the page table, pin counts and dirty flags
Trace LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep by hand on a small reference string and predict the victim
Explain sequential flooding and why recency alone cannot protect a hot set from a scan
Compute backward K-distances and pick the LRU-K victim
Compare 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers and choose one for a workload

lessons.title: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages

blocks.md:
In the prerequisite course a B-tree was a tree of fixed-size **pages** on disk, and every lookup walks root to leaf, reading one page per level. Reading a page from disk is far slower than reading it from RAM, so a database keeps recently used pages in memory and serves repeat reads from there.

That in-memory cache is the **buffer pool**. CMU's 15-445 notes describe it as an array of fixed-size **frames**, each able to hold one page, managed by the database itself rather than by the operating system.

Three pieces of bookkeeping make it work:

- The **page table**: an in-memory hash table from page id to the frame that holds it. Not to be confused with the on-disk page directory, which maps page ids to file locations.
- A **pin count** per frame: how many threads are using the page right now. A thread pins before it touches the page and unpins when done. A page with pin count above zero must not be evicted.
- A **dirty flag** per frame: set when a thread modifies the page. A dirty page must be written back to disk before its frame can be reused.

blocks.title: What happens when a query asks for page 42

nodes.label:
Page table
page id to frame

scenes.caption: The thread looks up page 42 in the page table. This is a hash lookup in memory, no disk involved.
Hit: the page is already in a frame. The thread pins it, uses it, and unpins it. Cost: a few memory accesses.
Miss and the pool is full: the replacer must choose a victim frame. Only unpinned frames qualify; the policy that picks among them is the subject of this course.
If the victim is dirty it must be written to disk first (the slow path). A clean victim is simply dropped (the fast path).
The page is read from disk into the freed frame, the page table now maps 42 to it, and the thread pins it. One miss cost one read and possibly one write.

blocks.md:
The *replacement policy* (also called the eviction policy) decides which unpinned page leaves when a new page needs a frame. It matters because the **hit rate**, the fraction of page requests served from memory, decides how often queries wait on disk.

The 2Q paper opens with the observation that fetching from disk takes at least a factor of 1000 more time than fetching from a RAM buffer. Use that ratio in a simple model: the average cost of one page access, in units of one memory access, is $h + (1-h)R$ for hit rate $h$ and miss penalty $R$.

blocks.title: Average page access cost vs hit rate

scenes.caption: With R = 1000, going from 90% to 99% hits cuts the average cost from 100.9 to 10.99, about 9x. Misses dominate the average long before the hit rate looks bad.

From 99% to 99.9% is another drop, to 1.999. Each extra nine matters, which is why a policy that wins a few percent of hit rate is worth real engineering. Simplified model: real costs also include writes of dirty victims.
R = 100 here: a faster device lowers the curve, and the labeled points (computed for R = 1000) no longer sit on it. Whenever R is much larger than 1, the miss term dominates.

blocks.md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

Why not just use the operating system's page cache through `mmap`? The CMU notes list the problems: the OS can flush dirty pages at any time (bad for transaction safety), a thread can stall on a page fault the database did not expect, I/O errors surface as signals, and the database knows its access patterns better than the OS. Owning the pool lets the database choose its own replacement policy, which is exactly what the rest of this course is about.

blocks.question: A pool has 4 frames. All 4 pages are pinned by running queries, and a fifth query misses on a new page. What should a correct buffer manager do?
options: Evict the least recently used page anyway, since it is the best guess
Report that no frame is available, or make the request wait, because pinned pages cannot be evicted
Evict any dirty page after writing it back, because writing makes eviction safe
Pick a random page, since all are equally valid victims
blocks.explain: Pinned means some thread is reading or writing that frame right now; evicting it would pull memory out from under that thread. PostgreSQL's clock-sweep raises the error "no unpinned buffers available" if it scans every buffer and all are pinned. Writing a dirty page back does not make it unpinned.

blocks.question: Two victims are equally old. Page X is clean, page Y is dirty. Why do many buffer managers prefer X?
options: Evicting X needs no disk write; evicting Y needs a write before the frame can be reused
Dirty pages are more likely to be accessed again soon
Clean pages take more memory than dirty pages
Y cannot be evicted until the transaction that dirtied it commits
blocks.explain: The clean page is the fast path: drop it and reuse the frame. The dirty page needs a write first, which is why systems run a background writer that cleans dirty pages ahead of eviction (PostgreSQL's bgwriter, for example).

lessons.title: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool

blocks.md:
**LRU** (least recently used) evicts the page whose last access is oldest. The idea: a page used recently will probably be used again soon (temporal locality). Implement it with a doubly linked list plus the page table: on every hit, unlink the page and move it to the most-recent end; on eviction, take the page at the least-recent end.

Watch it on a pool of 4 frames and the reference string A B C D A E B F A G.

scenes.caption: Step 1: A is a miss. A free frame takes it.
Step 2: B is a miss. A free frame takes it.
Step 3: C is a miss. A free frame takes it.
Step 4: D is a miss. A free frame takes it.
Step 5: A is a hit. A moves to the most recent end (right). Every hit reorders the list.
Step 6: E is a miss. The pool is full, so the least recently used page B (leftmost) is evicted.
Step 7: B is a miss. The pool is full, so the least recently used page C (leftmost) is evicted.
Step 8: F is a miss. The pool is full, so the least recently used page D (leftmost) is evicted.
Step 9: A is a hit. A moves to the most recent end (right). Every hit reorders the list.
Step 10: G is a miss. The pool is full, so the least recently used page E (leftmost) is evicted. Total: 2 hits out of 10.

blocks.md:
LRU's weakness in a database is not its choices but its cost. Every hit, even a read, rewrites the shared list. With many threads hitting the pool, they all contend for the latch (short-term lock) that protects that list.

**CLOCK** approximates LRU without the list. Frames sit in a circle, each with one **reference bit**, and a **clock hand** remembers its position between evictions. A hit sets the bit to 1. To evict, the hand sweeps: a frame with bit 1 gets a second chance (bit cleared to 0, move on); the first frame with bit 0 is the victim.

blocks.prompt: Same 4 frames, same string. After A B C D every bit is 1, and step 5 hits A (its bit stays 1). At step 6, E misses. Which page does CLOCK evict?
blocks.reveal: **A**, the page that was just hit. The hand starts at frame 0 and finds A, B, C, D all with bit 1. It clears all four, wraps around, and frame 0 (A) now has bit 0. When every bit is set, CLOCK cannot tell pages apart and degrades to FIFO. LRU would evict B here. One bit is a coarse summary of recency.

blocks.title: CLOCK on 4 frames, same reference string

scenes.caption: Step 1: A is a miss. It fills a free frame with its bit set to 1.
Step 2: B is a miss. It fills a free frame with its bit set to 1.
Step 3: C is a miss. It fills a free frame with its bit set to 1.
Step 4: D is a miss. It fills a free frame with its bit set to 1.
Step 5: A is a hit. Its reference bit is set to 1. Nothing moves: a hit is just one bit write.
Step 6: E misses. All four bits are 1, so the hand clears A, B, C, D in turn, wraps to frame 0, and evicts A, even though A was just hit. With every bit set, CLOCK behaves like FIFO.
Step 7: B is a hit. Its reference bit is set to 1. Nothing moves: a hit is just one bit write.
Step 8: F misses. The hand is at frame 1: B has bit 1 (it was hit at step 7), so B gets a second chance and its bit is cleared. C has bit 0 and is evicted.
Step 9: A is a miss. The hand finds D with bit 0 and evicts it.
Step 10: G misses. The hand is at frame 0: E has bit 1, so it is cleared and spared. B has bit 0 and is evicted. Total: 2 hits, same count as LRU here, but different victims.

blocks.md:
PostgreSQL's buffer manager uses a generalization called **clock-sweep**. Instead of one bit, each buffer has a `usage_count`. Pinning a buffer increments it, up to `BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT`, which is 5 in the source. The sweep decrements a nonzero count and moves on; it takes the first unpinned buffer whose count is already 0.

The source comment explains the cap: a large maximum would approximate LRU better, but finding a victim can take as many as `BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT + 1` complete cycles of the hand, so the value is kept small.

blocks.title: Clock-sweep picks a victim for E (usage counts capped at 5)

scenes.caption: Same string with usage counts. After A B C D and the hit on A, the counts are A=2, B=1, C=1, D=1 (a load sets 1, the hit on A adds 1). E misses; the hand is at frame 0.
Frame 0 holds A with usage 2. Not 0, so it is decremented to 1 and the hand moves on.
B, C and D each go from 1 to 0 as the hand passes. One full revolution done, nothing evicted yet.
Second lap: A goes from 1 to 0. A survives this eviction because its extra hit bought it one more lap.
B is unpinned with usage 0: it is the victim. Unlike plain CLOCK (which evicted A), the count remembered that A was used twice.
scenes.output: evict B, load E into frame 1

blocks.md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

blocks.question: Why does PostgreSQL cap `usage_count` at a small number like 5 rather than letting it grow without limit?
options: A larger cap would use too much memory per buffer header
With a larger cap, pinned buffers could be evicted
The sweep may need up to cap + 1 full laps to find a victim, so a large cap makes eviction slow
Counts above 5 overflow and wrap to 0
blocks.explain: The source comment says exactly this tradeoff: a large maximum approximates LRU, but each lap only decrements every count by one, so eviction could take as many as BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT + 1 complete cycles of the hand.

blocks.question: A pool serves 64 threads doing mostly read hits. Which policy causes the most contention, and why?
options: CLOCK, because every hit moves the hand
LRU with a shared linked list, because every hit must relink the page at the head under a latch
Clock-sweep, because every hit sweeps all buffers
None; replacement policies only run on misses
blocks.explain: Under LRU a hit is a write to a shared structure. Under CLOCK or clock-sweep a hit only sets a bit or bumps a per-buffer counter; the hand moves only on misses. Option 4 is the misconception: LRU's bookkeeping runs on every hit.

lessons.title: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set

blocks.md: LRU and CLOCK both assume that a page touched recently will be touched again. A large **sequential scan** breaks that assumption: it reads many pages exactly once, and each one becomes the most recently used page in the pool. The CMU notes call the result **sequential flooding**: the scan fills the pool with pages nobody will reread and pushes out the hot pages other queries need.

blocks.prompt: A pool has 4 frames, managed by LRU. A query loops over 5 pages, A B C D E, three times (15 references). How many hits?
blocks.reveal: **0 hits out of 15.** Every reference evicts exactly the page that will be needed soonest: E evicts A, then A evicts B, and so on. CLOCK also gets 0. A loop just one page larger than the pool is LRU's worst case, and it is the shape of a repeated scan over a table slightly bigger than memory.

blocks.title: Hot-page hit rate before and during a scan (simulated)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: 100 frames, a hot set of 60 pages read uniformly at random, plus 10% one-off reads of cold pages. Before any scan every policy keeps the hot set: 99.7% to 100.0% hits.

Now a 600-page scan runs, alternating one scan page with one hot read. LRU drops to 66.6% and CLOCK to 60.4%: each scan page enters as most recent and pushes out hot pages. Clock-sweep's counts help (74.1%).

LRU-2 and 2Q keep 100.0% and 100.0% of hot reads as hits: a page seen only once is the first to go, so scan pages evict each other. Averages over 5 random seeds; LRU-2 here keeps unlimited history, a simplification.

blocks.md: Why does clock-sweep with a cap of 5 do better than one-bit CLOCK? A hot page hit several times accumulates a count of up to 5, and the hand must pass it that many times before it can be evicted. A scan page enters with a count of 1 and is never touched again, so it becomes evictable after one pass. Frequency, not just recency, protects the hot set.

The CMU notes list three families of fixes:

1. **Track more history**, as LRU-K does: rank pages by their K-th most recent access, so a page touched once ranks below any page touched twice.
2. **Localize per query**: give a scan its own small set of frames so it recycles them instead of the whole pool. PostgreSQL's ring buffers (lesson 5) do this.
3. **Priority hints**: let the query executor tell the pool whether a page is worth keeping, for example index inner nodes versus table pages read by a scan.
Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

blocks.question: In the simulation, LRU loses more hot hits during the scan than clock-sweep with a cap of 5. What is the main reason?
options: Hot pages build up usage counts, so the hand must pass them several times before evicting them, while scan pages are evictable after one pass
Clock-sweep evicts scan pages first because it knows they are sequential
Clock-sweep has more frames than LRU in the simulation
LRU evicts dirty pages first
blocks.explain: Both policies have 100 frames and neither knows about scans. The difference is the counter: a page hit repeatedly survives several sweeps, while a page loaded once with count 1 is evictable after one sweep. It is still not perfect, which is why its bar does not reach 100%.

blocks.question: A nightly report scans a 50 GB table on a server whose buffer pool is 32 GB, under plain LRU. What happens to the next morning's OLTP queries?
options: Nothing; LRU keeps their pages because they were used more often
They get faster, because the pool is now warm
The scan fails because it does not fit in the pool
They see a burst of misses, because the scan's pages displaced their hot pages
blocks.explain: LRU only knows the time of the last reference. After the scan, the pool holds the most recent 32 GB of the scan, and the OLTP hot set has to be read back from disk. Frequency is invisible to plain LRU.

lessons.title: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference

blocks.md: O'Neil, O'Neil and Weikum (SIGMOD 1993) pinned LRU's problem down precisely: it decides what to drop based on too little information, only the time of the last reference. Their Example 1.1: random customer lookups through a B-tree, with 100 index leaf pages and 10,000 record pages, alternating leaf then record.

Each lookup hits one random leaf and one random record, so a given leaf page receives a fraction $0.5/100 = 0.005$ of all references, and a given record page only $0.5/10000 = 0.00005$, a hundred times less. With 101 frames the right choice is obvious: keep the root and all 100 leaves.

LRU keeps whatever was used most recently, which the paper estimates at roughly 50 leaf pages and 50 record pages. Half the pool goes to pages that are almost never reused.

blocks.tex: b_t(p,K) = t - (\text{time of the } K\text{-th most recent reference to } p), \qquad b_t(p,K)=\infty \text{ if } p \text{ has fewer than } K \text{ references}
blocks.caption: Backward K-distance at time t. LRU-K evicts the page in the pool with the largest b_t(p,K). K = 1 is plain LRU.

blocks.md:
Ties at infinity, pages seen fewer than K times, are broken by a subsidiary policy; the paper suggests classical LRU. The key effect: with K = 2 a page referenced once has infinite distance, so it is evicted before any page that has shown it gets reused.

Worked example: 3 frames, references A B A B C D E A B at times 1 to 9.

scenes.caption: After A B A B C (times 1 to 5) the pool holds A, B and C. A and B each have two references; C has one.
Time 6: D misses. b(A,2) = 6 minus 1 = 5, b(B,2) = 6 minus 2 = 4, b(C,2) is infinite because C has only one reference. Largest distance wins: evict C.
Plain LRU would have evicted A here (its last use, time 3, is the oldest). LRU-2 instead keeps both pages that showed reuse.
Time 7: E misses. b(A,2) = 6, b(B,2) = 5, b(D,2) is infinite. D goes. Pages referenced once leave first, like scan pages.
Times 8 and 9: A and B both hit. Totals for this string: LRU-2 gets 4 hits, LRU gets 2 (LRU evicted A at time 6 and B at time 7).

blocks.md:
Two refinements make LRU-K usable on real traces:

- **Correlated Reference Period**: several references in quick succession (one transaction reading a page, then updating it) are collapsed into one, so a burst does not masquerade as long-term popularity.
- **Retained Information Period**: the history of a page is kept for a while *after* it is evicted, so a page that returns can be recognized as reused. The paper suggests about 200 seconds, twice the roughly 100-second interarrival time that the Five Minute Rule gives for a 4 KB page.

The results: in the two-pool experiment with 60 buffer pages, LRU-2 reaches a hit ratio of 0.291, and LRU-1 needs about 140 pages to match it, a ratio of 140 / 60 = 2.3. LRU-3 comes even closer to the optimal policy on stable patterns but adapts more slowly when access frequencies change, so the authors advocate K = 2.

The price is bookkeeping. Choosing the page with the largest backward distance needs a priority queue, which the 2Q paper describes as log N work per access for a pool of N pages, plus history entries for evicted pages.

LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

blocks.question: At time 20 a pool holds P (references at 4, 15, 19), Q (references at 12, 17) and R (one reference at 18). Under LRU-2, which page is evicted?
options: P, because its oldest reference (time 4) is the oldest in the pool
Q, because b(Q,2) = 8 is larger than b(P,2) = 5
R, because it has only one reference, so b(R,2) is infinite
Q, because its last reference is the oldest
blocks.explain: b(P,2) = 20 minus 15 = 5 (second most recent is 15, not 4). b(Q,2) = 20 minus 12 = 8. R has one reference, so its distance is infinite and it goes first. Option 2 would be right if R were not in the pool.

blocks.question: Why do O'Neil et al. recommend K = 2 rather than K = 3 for general use?
options: K = 3 never beats K = 2 on any workload
K = 3 cannot be implemented with a priority queue
K = 3 turns into plain LRU when the pool is large
K = 3 needs more references before it adapts when access frequencies change
blocks.explain: The paper reports that LRU-3 comes closer to the optimal policy on stable patterns, but it needs more references to adapt to changing frequencies. K = 2 is the practical balance.

lessons.title: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers

blocks.md:
Johnson and Shasha (VLDB 1994) asked whether LRU-2's benefit could be had at constant cost per access, like LRU. Their answer is **2Q**. Instead of cleaning cold pages out of the main buffer, 2Q only *admits* pages that have proven themselves.

The full version keeps three queues:

- **A1in**: a FIFO of pages seen once recently, holding real pages (at most Kin of them).
- **A1out**: a FIFO of *identifiers* of pages recently paged out of A1in. No page data, only a few bytes each.
- **Am**: an LRU queue of pages that were referenced again after leaving A1in.

On a miss for a page in A1out, the page goes to Am. A hit while still in A1in does nothing, because a quick second access may just be a correlated reference. When a frame is needed, 2Q pages out the tail of A1in if A1in is larger than Kin, otherwise the tail of Am.

The paper's suggested values: Kin = 25% of the page slots, and Kout = identifiers for as many pages as would fit in 50% of the buffer. For a 1000-frame pool that is Kin = 250 pages and Kout = 500 remembered ids.

scenes.caption: A misses and fills a free frame. Every first-time page enters A1in, a FIFO; B, C and D will follow the same way.
The pool (4 frames) is full. All four pages sit in A1in, which is far above Kin = 1.
E misses. A1in is over Kin, so its oldest page A is paged out, and only A's identifier goes to A1out. E enters A1in.
A is requested again. It is a miss, but A is found in A1out: it was reused after leaving, so it is promoted to Am. B is paged out of A1in to make room.
A scan begins: W enters A1in and pushes C out of A1in.
X enters A1in; D is paged out. Scan pages only ever replace other A1in pages while A1in is over Kin.
Y enters; the oldest identifier is dropped from A1out once it exceeds Kout = 2.
Z enters. Four scan pages have passed through, yet Am still holds A.
A hits in Am. 2Q: 1 hit on this string. LRU on the same 4 frames gets 0: the four scan pages pushed A out.

blocks.md: A1out is cheap memory for a strong signal. Remembering that a page was here recently costs a few bytes, yet it is exactly what lets 2Q (and LRU-K's retained history) recognize the second reference that separates hot pages from one-off reads.

**InnoDB** (MySQL) uses a related idea, midpoint insertion. Its LRU list is split into a *new* (young) sublist and an *old* sublist. Pages read from disk are inserted at the head of the old sublist, not at the head of the whole list. The system variable `innodb_old_blocks_pct` sets the old share; its default in the source is `100 * 3 / 8`, which is 37 in integer arithmetic.

A page in the old sublist is moved to the young end on access only if its first access was at least `innodb_old_blocks_time` milliseconds ago, default 1000. A scan that touches a page several times in a burst therefore does not promote it.

nodes.label:
Accessed again
1000 ms or more later?

scenes.caption: A new page enters at the midpoint: the head of the old sublist. It never jumps straight to the most-recent end of the whole list.
Pages of a scan that are not touched again simply drift to the tail of the old sublist and are evicted. The young sublist, where the hot set lives, is untouched.
A page re-accessed while old is made young only if its first access was at least innodb_old_blocks_time (default 1000 ms) earlier. Rapid repeat reads by one scan do not count.

blocks.md:
**PostgreSQL** keeps clock-sweep for normal access and adds *buffer access strategies* (ring buffers) for operations that touch many pages once. Its buffer README describes a 256 KB ring for large sequential scans, which is 32 buffers of 8 KB; the scan recycles its own ring instead of flooding `shared_buffers`. Pins through a ring raise `usage_count` to 1 at most, so ring pages stay easy to evict. Current source can enlarge the scan ring to leave room for asynchronous I/O.

VACUUM uses a ring sized by `vacuum_buffer_usage_limit` (default 2 MB), and bulk writes such as `COPY IN` use 16 MB, capped at 1/8 of `shared_buffers`.

Dirty pages interact with the ring. If a scan dirties a ring buffer, reusing it would first require flushing WAL, so the scan drops that buffer from the ring and gets a replacement from the normal clock-sweep. The README notes the consequence: for a bulk `UPDATE` or `DELETE` that dirties every page, the ring strategy effectively degrades to the normal strategy.

Separately, PostgreSQL's **background writer** scans ahead of the clock hand for dirty, unpinned buffers with a zero usage count and writes them out, so that backends usually find clean victims.

Real systems combine a cheap recency approximation with a second signal: PostgreSQL uses counts plus per-operation rings, InnoDB uses a two-segment list with a time threshold, and 2Q and LRU-2 use a remembered first reference. The common goal: a page must prove reuse before it can displace the hot set.

blocks.question: In 2Q, a page in A1in is referenced a second time while still in A1in. What happens?
options: Nothing: it stays in A1in, because a quick second reference may be correlated
It moves to the head of Am, since two references prove it is hot
Its identifier is copied to A1out
It is evicted, because A1in only holds pages seen once
blocks.explain: The full 2Q algorithm deliberately ignores hits in A1in. Only a reference after the page has been paged out to A1out, that is after some time has passed, promotes it to Am. This is 2Q's version of LRU-K's correlated reference period.

blocks.question: A PostgreSQL job runs `UPDATE big_table SET flag = true` over every row of a table much larger than shared_buffers. Why can it still pollute the buffer pool despite ring buffers?
options: Ring buffers are only used for indexes
UPDATE always bypasses shared_buffers
Each ring buffer it uses gets dirtied, and a dirtied scan buffer is dropped from the ring and replaced through normal clock-sweep, so the ring degrades to the normal strategy
The ring is larger than shared_buffers
blocks.explain: The README says this directly: a scan that modifies every page dirties every ring buffer, and rather than flushing WAL to reuse it, the buffer is discarded from the ring and a replacement comes from the normal clock-sweep.

blocks.question: You are designing a page cache for a key-value store whose workload mixes point lookups with frequent full scans, and you want O(1) work per access. Which policy fits best?
options: Plain LRU
LRU-2 with a priority queue
2Q, or a midpoint-insertion LRU like InnoDB's
CLOCK with one reference bit
blocks.explain: Plain LRU and one-bit CLOCK flood on scans. LRU-2 resists scans but costs log N per access for the priority queue. 2Q and midpoint insertion both admit pages to the hot region only after evidence of reuse, at constant cost per access.
